claim: AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry transduced V1 GABAergic neurons in a marmoset with 93% selectivity in a previous study.
source: A previous study showed that an AAV vector carrying the gene for the fluorescent reporter, GFP, under the control of the mDlx5/6 enhancer, transduced V1 GABAergic neurons in a marmoset with 93% selectivity (Dimidschstein et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dimidschstein et al., 2016.

claim: mCherry-positive cells had non-pyramidal morphologies in macaque V1.
source: mCherry-positive cells had non-pyramidal morphologies, consistent with them being GABAergic.
evidence: The claim is based on histological observations from the study.

claim: Most mCherry-positive neurons co-expressed parvalbumin (468/543).
source: Most mCherry-positive neurons co-expressed parvalbumin (468/543), a marker for 75% of GABAergic neurons in macaque V1 (Van Brederode et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from histological analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Parvalbumin is a marker for 75% of GABAergic neurons in macaque V1.
source: Most mCherry-positive neurons co-expressed parvalbumin (468/543), a marker for 75% of GABAergic neurons in macaque V1 (Van Brederode et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Brederode et al., 1990.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive neurons were transduced with particularly high efficiency (p<0.005).
source: This high level of co-expression is consistent with selective transduction of GABAergic neurons and is sufficiently high to suggest that parvalbumin-positive neurons were transduced with particularly high efficiency (p<0.005; binomial test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (binomial test) of the histological data.

claim: Most recording sites were visually driven (46/56).
source: Most sites were visually driven (46/56, response to a low-contrast Gabor stimulus greater than baseline firing rate; 19/56, p<0.05; Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data and statistical testing.

claim: At 38 of the 56 sites, optical stimulation increased spiking.
source: At 38 of the 56 sites, optical stimulation increased spiking.
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings during optical stimulation.

claim: The mean latency to response was 14±26 (SD) ms.
source: The mean latency to response was 14±26 (SD) ms and was <5 ms at 11 sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Latency to response was <5 ms at 11 sites.
source: The mean latency to response was 14±26 (SD) ms and was <5 ms at 11 sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons excited at short latency (<5 ms) presumably expressed ChR2 and suppressed other neurons via synaptic inhibition.
source: Neurons excited at short latency (<5 ms) presumably expressed ChR2 and suppressed other neurons via synaptic inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the short latency of excitation.

claim: Neural activity suppression using halorhodopsins in monkeys is typically followed by a rebound of activity at the termination of optical stimulation.
source: Neural activity suppression using halorhodopsins in monkeys is typically followed by a rebound of activity at the termination of optical stimulation (Acker et al., 2016; Fetsch et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rebound activity was not observed with AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2.
source: We did not observe such rebounds with AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of electrophysiological data from the current study.

claim: Post-laser firing rates exceeded pre-laser firing rates at only 2 of 18 sites.
source: Such rebounds were rare; post-laser firing rates exceeded pre-laser firing rates at only 2 of 18 sites (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Recovery times ranged from 0 to 215 ms with a median of 97.5 ms.
source: Recovery times ranged from 0 to 215 ms (Figure 3D) with roughly half of the sites recovering within 100 ms (median = 97.5 ms).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of recovery times shown in Figure 3D.

claim: On laser trials, both monkeys failed to make saccades into the RFs of the optically stimulated neurons.
source: On laser trials, the monkeys failed to make saccades into the RFs of the optically stimulated neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from the visually guided saccade task.

claim: Saccades were unaffected when the target appeared at locations outside the RFs.
source: Saccades were unaffected when the target appeared at other locations, indicating that the optogenetic effect was retinotopically specific.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data demonstrating spatial specificity.

claim: When the target appeared inside the RFs of stimulated neurons, saccade end points tended to be closer to the target on control trials than on laser trials (p<0.002 for monkey 2, p=0.03 for monkey 3).
source: When the target appeared inside the RFs of stimulated neurons, the saccade end points tended to be closer to the target on control trials than on laser trials (p<0.002 for monkey 2, p=0.03 for monkey 3; Wilcoxon signed rank tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Saccade latencies were greater on laser trials than on control trials when targets were inside the RFs (p<0.0001 for monkey 2 and 3).
source: Saccade latencies were greater on laser trials than on control trials when targets were inside the RFs (p<0.0001 for monkey 2 and 3; Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D) but not when targets were elsewhere (p=0.90 for monkey 2 and p=0.41 for monkey 3; Mann-Whitney U tests; Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both monkeys detected the visual stimulus more frequently on control than on laser trials (p<0.001 for both monkeys).
source: Both monkeys detected the visual stimulus more frequently on control than on laser trials (proportion of hits on control vs. laser trials; p<0.001 for monkey 2 and monkey 3; binomial tests for equality of proportions; Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neither monkey was able to detect the visual stimulus with above-chance accuracy on laser trials even at the maximum stimulus contrast achievable.
source: Neither monkey was able to detect the visual stimulus with above-chance accuracy on laser trials even at the maximum stimulus contrast achievable.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral performance data from the contrast detection task.

claim: In almost every session (10/11 in monkey 2, 11/12 in monkey 3), the proportion of hits on control trials was significantly greater than on laser trials (p<0.05).
source: In almost every session (10/11 in monkey 2, 11/12 in monkey 3), the proportion of hits on control trials was significantly greater than on laser trials (binomial tests for equality of proportions, p<0.05, Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis across multiple sessions shown in Figure 7.

claim: In most blocks of trials (52/69 in monkey 2 and 63/81 in monkey 3), optical stimulation increased detection thresholds beyond the limits of the display.
source: In most blocks of trials (52/69 in monkey 2 and 63/81 in monkey 3), optical stimulation increased detection thresholds beyond the limits of the display, an event that occurred rarely on control trials (0/63 blocks in monkey 2, 8/81 blocks in monkey 3).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of behavioral data across multiple blocks.

claim: The magnitude of the behavioral effect increased steeply with laser intensity between 12.8 and 22.3 mW, and it saturated by 30.0 mW.
source: The magnitude of the behavioral effect increased steeply with laser intensity between 12.8 and 22.3 mW, and it saturated by 30.0 mW (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral effects as a function of laser power shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Behavior on control trials was not significantly affected by changes in laser power (r=−0.15, p=0.78).
source: Behavior on control trials was not significantly affected by changes in laser power (r=−0.15, p=0.78; Spearman's correlation between d' on control trials from each block and laser power).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The behavioral effects were consistently large over the course of ~1000 trials (or ~50 mins).
source: The behavioral effects we observed were consistently large over the course of ~1000 trials (or ~50 mins).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral data across extended sessions.

claim: The behavioral effect varied little as a function of block number (r=0.18, p=0.59).
source: The behavioral effect varied little as a function of block number, (r=0.18, p=0.59; Spearman's correlation between block number and d' averaged across sessions; Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The behavioral effect did not differ between the first 480 trials and the subsequent trials (p=0.79).
source: Unlike the previous work, the behavioral effect did not differ between the first 480 trials (4 blocks) and the subsequent trials, suggesting the absence of compensatory changes under the conditions of the current study (p=0.79, Student's t-test, Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Optogenetics is the fastest method for reversible neural inactivation currently available.
source: Optogenetics is the fastest method for reversible neural inactivation currently available.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about optogenetic methods.

claim: In rodents, optogenetic inactivation has revealed links between neural activity and behavior that would have been difficult to discover with traditional, slower inactivation methods.
source: In rodents, optogenetic inactivation has revealed links between neural activity and behavior that would have been difficult to discover with traditional, slower inactivation methods based on injection of pharmacological agents, cortical cooling, or lesioning (Goshen et al., 2011; Hanks et al., 2015; Yartsev et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in rodents.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation has been used in a few pioneering studies to perturb the behavior of macaque monkeys.
source: Optogenetic inactivation has already been used in a few pioneering studies to perturb the behavior of macaque monkeys (Acker et al., 2016; Afraz et al., 2015; Cavanaugh et al., 2012; Fetsch et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in macaques.

claim: The behavioral effects produced by direct hyperpolarization of neurons with opsins have been small, perhaps because suppression of inhibitory neurons may counteract suppression of excitatory neurons.
source: However, the behavioral effects produced this way have been small, perhaps because most promoters used in viral vectors drive expression in many neuronal types, and suppression of inhibitory neurons may counteract suppression of excitatory neurons.
evidence: The claim involves speculation about the reasons for small behavioral effects.

claim: Selective activation of inhibitory neurons with ChR2 has been successful in rodents.
source: An alternative approach, which has been successful in rodents, is to selectively activate inhibitory neurons with channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) (Cone et al., 2019; Glickfeld et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014; Khan et al., 2018; McBride et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in rodents.

claim: ChR2-based approaches have two advantages: they are based on ion channels which conduct more ions per photon absorbed than ion pumps, and they leverage the dense local connectivity and low synaptic failure rates of GABAergic neurons.
source: This approach has two advantages. First, it is based on the opening of ion channels, which conduct more ions per photon absorbed than ion pumps. Second, it leverages the dense local connectivity and low synaptic failure rates of GABAergic neurons to suppress long-range excitatory signaling locally and robustly (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Kubota et al., 2015; Packer and Yuste, 2011; Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and established knowledge.

claim: Illumination of ChR2-expressing neurons in area V1 causes monkeys to make saccades into the RFs of the stimulated neurons under some conditions.
source: Illumination of ChR2-expressing neurons in area V1 causes monkeys to make saccades into the RFs of the stimulated neurons under some conditions (Jazayeri et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jazayeri et al., 2012.

claim: In the current study, monkeys rarely made saccades into the RFs of the stimulated neurons, suggesting that they did not experience a phosphene.
source: In our study, however, monkeys rarely made saccades into the RFs of the stimulated neurons, suggesting that they did not experience a phosphene.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations and inference.

claim: The difference between studies is attributed to the population of V1 neurons stimulated.
source: We attribute the difference between studies to the population of V1 neurons stimulated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design differences.

claim: Jazayeri et al., 2012 used the human synapsin I promoter, which drives expression in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: We used a Dlx5/6 enhancer to express ChR2 selectively in inhibitory neurons whereas Jazayeri et al., 2012 used the human synapsin I promoter, which drives expression in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Nathanson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nathanson et al., 2009.

claim: One hypothesis is that phosphenes are caused by spikes in a subset of excitatory projection neurons.
source: One hypothesis is that phosphenes are caused by spikes in a subset of excitatory projection neurons.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Over the course of this study, monkeys 2 and 3 acquired visual deficits in areas of the visual field corresponding to the regions of V1 inactivated.
source: Over the course of this study, monkeys 2 and 3 acquired visual deficits in areas of the visual field corresponding to the regions of V1 inactivated.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations over time.

claim: Visual sensitivity was reduced in the optogenetically manipulated lower-right visual field relative to the unmanipulated upper-left visual field in monkey 2 twenty-two months after the final optogenetic experiment, but the deficit was subtle.
source: Visual sensitivity, assessed by the probability, latency, and accuracy of visually guided saccades, was reduced in the optogenetically manipulated lower-right visual field relative to the unmanipulated upper-left visual field, but the deficit was subtle.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data collected 22 months after experiments.

claim: The deficit is presumed to reflect cortical damage, which could be due to tissue heating by the light, repeated penetrations by optical fibers, or single-unit recordings.
source: We presume that this deficit reflects cortical damage, which could be due to tissue heating by the light, repeated penetrations by optical fibers, or single-unit recordings that were made in this animal for three years prior to commencing the current study.
evidence: The claim involves speculation about the causes of the observed deficit.

claim: The laser power used in the current study spanned a broad range (4–160 mW for 200–300 ms) and was higher than that used in other studies.
source: The laser power used in the current study spanned a broad range (4–160 mW for 200–300 ms) and, on average, was higher than that used in other studies (Afraz et al., 2015; Cavanaugh et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2014; El-Shamayleh et al., 2017; Fetsch et al., 2018; Gerits et al., 2012; Inoue et al., 2015; Ohayon et al., 2013; Stauffer et al., 2016; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with cited studies.

claim: Given the stimulation parameters used, tissue near the fiber tip was likely heated by several °C in many experiments.
source: Given the stimulation parameters we used, (450 nm light conducted through 300 µm-diameter optical fibers), we likely heated tissue near the fiber tip by several °C in many of our experiments (Arias-Gil et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from stimulation parameters and a citation.

claim: The consistency of the behavioral effect within individual sessions after repeated optical stimulation argues against acute damage.
source: However, the consistency of the behavioral effect within individual sessions after repeated optical stimulation argues against acute damage (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 8C–D.

claim: Tissue damage produced by optogenetic manipulations can be mitigated by using artificial dura and red-shifted or step-function opsins.
source: The tissue damage produced by optogenetic manipulations can be mitigated by using artificial dura (Nandy et al., 2019; Ruiz et al., 2013) and red-shifted or step-function opsins (Berndt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Artificial dura allows non-invasive optical stimulation of the superficial cortical layers, reducing mechanical damage.
source: Artificial dura allows non-invasive optical stimulation of the superficial cortical layers, reducing mechanical damage.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about artificial dura.

claim: Red-shifted opsins are activated by long-wavelength light, which heats tissue less and thus causes less thermal damage than short-wavelength lights do.
source: Red-shifted opsins are activated by long-wavelength light, which heats tissue less and thus causes less thermal damage than short-wavelength lights do.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about opsin properties.

claim: The neural activity produced by step-function opsins outlast the light pulses required to trigger them, allowing brief, safe light pulses to produce longer lasting stimulation events.
source: The neural activity produced by step-function opsins outlast the light pulses required to trigger them, allowing brief, safe light pulses to produce longer lasting stimulation events (Gong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gong et al., 2020.

claim: Threshold changes observed in this study were larger than those in previous studies (~5% vs. >100%).
source: In both cases, threshold changes were smaller than those we observed (~5% vs. >100%, Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of behavioral effects with previous studies.

claim: The large threshold changes were potentially due to several reasons including exciting ChR2-expressing inhibitory neurons, using ChR2 which conducts more ions per absorbed photon than ion pumps, using higher laser power, and inactivating area V1 which is indispensable for the behaviors studied.
source: The threshold changes we observed were large for potentially several reasons. First, we excited ChR2-expressing inhibitory neurons to reduce the spiking of excitatory neurons. Stimulation of a small number of inhibitory neurons can suppress the activity of a large number of excitatory neurons (Wiegert et al., 2017). Second, we used ChR2, which conducts more ions per absorbed photon than ion pumps (Jaws and ArchT). Third, we used higher laser power (4–160 mW vs. ~2 mW and ~12 mW; Figures 4–8). Fourth, we inactivated area V1, an area that is indispensable for the behaviors we studied (Koerner and Teuber, 1973; Merigan et al., 1993; Radoeva et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim involves inference and speculation about the reasons for large behavioral effects, supported by citations.

claim: Higher-order visual cortical areas may be sufficiently interconnected to allow one or more areas to compensate for others with regard to the behaviors tested.
source: Higher-order visual cortical areas may be sufficiently interconnected to allow one or more areas to compensate for others with regard to the behaviors tested.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the organization of higher-order visual areas.

claim: An intriguing hypothesis is that the spared visual sensitivity following visual cortical lesions is due to the engagement of slow compensatory mechanisms, not the unmasking of normally functioning pathways.
source: An intriguing, and now-testable, hypothesis is that the spared visual sensitivity following visual cortical lesions is due to the engagement of slow compensatory mechanisms, not the unmasking of normally functioning pathways (Leopold, 2012).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a hypothesis and supported by a citation.

claim: The stimulation-induced change in the monkeys' performance was interpreted as a change in sensitivity, inconsistent with a change in criterion alone.
source: We interpreted the stimulation-induced change in the monkeys' performance as a change in sensitivity, and it is inconsistent with a change in criterion alone.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral data using signal detection theory.

claim: The brevity and unpredictability of the optical stimulation makes large, consistent, selective changes in criterion on laser trials unlikely.
source: Additionally, the brevity and unpredictability of the optical stimulation makes large, consistent, selective changes in criterion on laser trials unlikely.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons within a cortical area have different response properties in mice, cats, and ferrets.
source: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons within a cortical area have different response properties in mice, cats, and ferrets, a fact that is presumably related to differences in their respective functional contributions (Huang and Paul, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huang and Paul, 2018.

claim: Identification of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in vivo has been challenging in monkeys.
source: Identification of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in vivo has been challenging in monkeys.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about technical challenges.

claim: The discovery of fast-spiking excitatory neurons in primates undermines the use of extracellularly recorded spike waveforms for cell type identification.
source: The discovery of fast-spiking excitatory neurons in primates undermines the use of extracellularly recorded spike waveforms (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: Optogenetic phototagging of inhibitory neurons using AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 permits electrophysiological identification of neuronal subtypes more decisively.
source: Optogenetic phototagging of inhibitory neurons, using AAV–mDlx5/6–ChR2 permits electrophysiological identification of neuronal subtypes more decisively (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons is a powerful method for inactivating regions of the macaque monkey brain with high spatial and temporal precision.
source: We conclude that optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons is a powerful method for inactivating regions of the macaque monkey brain with high spatial and temporal precision.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, based on all the data presented.

claim: This inhibitory cell-type-specific optogenetic approach is a powerful and spatiotemporally precise neural inactivation tool with broad utility for probing the functional contributions of cortical activity in macaques.
source: We conclude that this inhibitory cell-type-specific optogenetic approach is a powerful and spatiotemporally precise neural inactivation tool with broad utility for probing the functional contributions of cortical activity in macaques.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as the main conclusion.

claim: Optical stimulation modulated spiking activity in the region of space represented by the stimulated neurons.
source: Optical stimulation modulated spiking activity and reduced visual sensitivity profoundly in the region of space represented by the stimulated neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Optical stimulation reduced visual sensitivity profoundly in the region of space represented by the stimulated neurons.
source: Optical stimulation modulated spiking activity and reduced visual sensitivity profoundly in the region of space represented by the stimulated neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from the contrast detection task.

claim: The efficacy of the optogenetic manipulation on behavior was maintained across >1000 trials.
source: Rebound firing, which can have unwanted effects on neural circuits following inactivation, was not observed, and the efficacy of the optogenetic manipulation on behavior was maintained across >1000 trials.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral data across extended sessions.

claim: Three rhesus monkeys (males; 7–14 kg) participated in this study.
source: Three rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in this study (males; 7–14 kg).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Two monkeys were surgically implanted with a head-holding device and a recording chamber that provided access to the primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Two monkeys were surgically implanted with a head-holding device and a recording chamber that provided access to the primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: The claim describes the surgical procedures.

claim: In monkey 2, 14 μL of AAV9–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry (1.5 × 10^13 genomes/ml) was injected at each of two opercular sites that were ~2 mm apart.
source: In monkey 2, we injected 14 μL of AAV9–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry (1.5 × 1013 genomes/ml) at each of two opercular sites that were ~2 mm apart.
evidence: The claim describes the injection procedure.

claim: In monkey 3, ~17 μL of AAV1–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry (1.0 × 10^13 genomes/ml) was injected along a 5 mm track in the first site and 14 μL along a 6.5 mm track in the second site.
source: In monkey 3, we injected ~17 μL of AAV1–mDlx5/6–ChR2–mCherry (1.0 × 1013 genomes/ml) along a 5 mm track in the first site and 14 μL along a 6.5 mm track in the second site, in the right hemisphere, to target both opercular and calcarine regions of area V1.
evidence: The claim describes the injection procedure.

claim: Monkey 1 was euthanized 45 days after AAV injection.
source: The monkey recovered from the surgery and was euthanized 45 days later with an overdose of pentobarbital and perfused transcardially with 4% paraformaldehyde (wt/vol).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental timeline.

claim: Three to four weeks after AAV injections in monkeys 2 and 3, neuronal responses to blue light were searched for.
source: Three to four weeks after AAV injections in monkeys 2 and 3, we searched for neuronal responses to blue light (450 nm; 33–161 mW) delivered to area V1 via an optical fiber (300 μm outer diameter; Thor Labs) with a beveled tip that eased entry through the dura.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental timeline and procedures.

claim: Stimulation sites were selected by finding a region with vigorous visual activity and a clearly defined receptive field.
source: Stimulation sites were selected by inserting an electrode into V1 and finding a region with vigorous visual activity and a clearly defined receptive field (RF).
evidence: The claim describes the site selection criteria.

claim: Only sites at which optical stimulation produced an audible change in firing rate were tested.
source: Only sites at which optical stimulation produced an audible change in firing rate were tested.
evidence: The claim describes the site selection criteria.

claim: Sensitivity (d') was measured using a standard formula from signal detection theory.
source: Sensitivity (d') was measured using a standard formula from signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966; Macmillan and Creelman, 2004).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis method and is supported by citations.

claim: Proportions of correct responses were fit with a cumulative Weibull distribution function by maximizing likelihood assuming binomial error.
source: Proportions of correct responses were fit with a cumulative Weibull distribution function by maximizing likelihood assuming binomial error.
evidence: The claim describes the analysis method.

claim: Detection threshold was defined as the luminance contrast corresponding to 82% correct.
source: Detection threshold was defined as the luminance contrast corresponding to 82% correct.
evidence: The claim describes the definition used in the analysis.
